addressed_problems.content: The LTH-IMP pipeline used to locate winning Trojan tickets involves multiple cycles of iterative magnitude pruning, retraining, and linear mode connectivity evaluation, which is computationally expensive. A key open problem is how to scale this approach to substantially larger and deeper models, such as very large ImageNet-scale architectures, without prohibitive cost. Future work must develop more efficient algorithms or approximations to make the method practical for routine inspection of large third-party models, while preserving the detection and recovery performance demonstrated on moderate-scale networks.

The method exhibits documented failure cases in which the LMC-based Trojan score does not accurately locate the winning Trojan ticket: for clean-label attacks, 3 out of 10 replicates with different random seeds fail, and for unpoisoned datasets, 2 out of 10 trials yield a false positive detection. An unresolved issue is whether the approach can be made robust across all attacker variants, trigger types, and random seeds. Understanding the conditions under which the peak Trojan score fails to correspond to the true winning Trojan ticket, and developing remedies to guarantee reliable detection, remains an open challenge.

The success of the proposed Trojan detection and trigger recovery depends on several pruning hyperparameters and design choices. The per-round prune fraction p must be chosen carefully: p=10% or 20% work, but p=40% can fail to preserve Trojan information. Additionally, the number of fine-tuning steps k (set to 10 in experiments) affects detection reliability, and the pruning algorithm itself matters — random pruning fails, while LTH, OMP, and SNIP succeed. A systematic understanding of which pruning schedules, mask structures, and algorithmic choices yield universally effective winning Trojan tickets is lacking. Future work should investigate principled guidelines for setting these parameters and whether adaptive or data-driven pruning policies can eliminate the need for manual tuning.

The empirical results show that Trojan features are significantly more stable to extreme magnitude pruning than benign features, leading to a winning Trojan ticket that preserves high ASR while near-random SA. However, a theoretical explanation for this phenomenon is not provided. Visualizations of loss landscapes indicate that winning Trojan tickets often exhibit sharp local minima, suggesting a connection between geometry and Trojan retention, but the causal mechanism remains unclear. An unresolved scientific question is why sparsity preferentially retains backdoor information, and how the sparse connectivity pattern itself encodes the Trojan trigger. Developing a formal understanding would strengthen the foundation of sparsity-based Trojan detection and potentially guide more principled pruning strategies.

The method is designed to defend against malicious Trojan attacks by enabling model suppliers to inspect third-party models without clean data. However, as the authors acknowledge, the same technique could potentially be misused by adversaries to create more stealthy backdoors or to evade detection. The computational overhead of the pruning pipeline may also limit its practical deployment for routine model inspection. Open issues include establishing operational safeguards (such as strict licensing) to prevent dual-use, studying adversarial countermeasures where attackers adapt to sparsity-based detection, and developing more efficient variants that can be integrated into standard model release pipelines without imposing prohibitive costs.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to training-time backdoor (Trojan) attacks in which an adversary poisons a small fraction of the training data so that the model behaves normally on clean inputs but produces attacker-chosen outputs whenever a particular input-agnostic trigger is present. Detecting whether a delivered model contains such a backdoor and recovering the trigger are both challenging when the defender has no access to any clean (unpoisoned) training or validation data. Prior defenses that recover triggers (e.g., Neural Cleanse) or mitigate backdoors often rely on access to some clean images, assume knowledge about the threat model, or use indirect heuristics; pruning- or sparsity-based works either do not connect pruning behavior clearly to Trojan persistence or assume idealized access (e.g., clean finetuning data) that masks whether sparsity itself is the cause of mitigation. Separately, the lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) and iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) show that extreme sparsification can expose sparse subnetworks (winning tickets) with characteristic optimization behavior, but these results were developed for non-poisoned training and it is unknown how pruning dynamics interact with Trojan features when the pruner is blind to poisoning. Because of these gaps, practitioners lack (i) a principled, data-free way to detect whether a provided model contains an embedded Trojan trigger; (ii) a reliable route to recover that trigger without clean images; and (iii) an understanding of whether and how model sparsity (found by LTH-style pruning) preserves or isolates Trojan information rather than only preserving benign generalization. These limitations prevent trustworthy inspection of third-party models and leave open whether sparsity-aware tools can enable detection and trigger recovery under the realistic constraint of zero access to clean training data.

nodes.content: In the context of Trojan-infected models, defenders need a pruning and analysis workflow that (i) can be executed without any access to clean validation data and (ii) isolates the effect of sparsity on Trojan features rather than conflating sparsification with subsequent clean-data finetuning. Prior LTH/IMP practice and pruning-based defenses either assume clean finetuning, study only benign generalization, or do not examine the distinct behaviors of pruned-but-unfinetuned versus pruned-and-finetuned subnetworks when the training data may be poisoned. Without a principled pruning regime tailored to Trojan models, one cannot reliably determine whether sparsity preserves or destroys backdoor information, nor can one form a pipeline that leverages sparsity to detect or recover triggers under the practical constraint of zero clean data.

A practical Trojan detector that requires no clean images must distinguish pruning behavior caused by ordinary optimization noise from pruning behavior that reflects preserved backdoor correlations. Existing connectivity or LTH observations apply to non-poisoned settings and imply near-zero LMC-based barriers among IMP-derived subnetworks; they do not offer an operational detection statistic that signals the presence of a Trojan when only poisoned data are available. Consequently, defenders lacked a scalar, model-intrinsic metric that can be computed along a pruning trajectory to pinpoint subnetworks that disproportionately retain backdoor behavior even when benign accuracy collapses. The proposed Trojan score fills this gap by formalizing a connectivity-based stability measure that is sensitive to the asymmetric effect of fine-tuning on Trojan-versus-benign features.

For defenders to exploit sparsity to detect or reverse-engineer Trojans, it must be known whether extreme sparsification can actually preserve backdoor function while destroying benign generalization so that backdoor features become isolated and thus analyzable. Prior work had mixed or indirect evidence about pruning’s effect on backdoors and often conflated pruning with clean-data finetuning. Without an empirical demonstration that (a) such sparse subnetworks exist reproducibly across architectures, datasets, and attack types and (b) they are detectable by an objective (Trojan score) along an IMP path, there is no practical route to isolate Trojan information via pruning. The reported existence and reproducibility of winning Trojan tickets supply the necessary empirical validation that sparsity can reveal a backdoor-preserving subnetwork under realistic, data-free conditions.

Existing trigger-recovery defenses either fail often (unstable target detection, low-quality recovered triggers) or require benign images to drive the reverse-optimization, which may be unavailable. There was no demonstrated, practical way to run reverse-engineering without clean data and still obtain a trigger with high ASR and correct target-label detection, especially against harder clean-label attacks. Because winning Trojan tickets concentrate Trojan information while removing benign accuracy, they offer a candidate victim model that makes the inverse optimization problem easier and input-agnostic. The data-free recovery pipeline using noise images therefore resolves the gap of how to recover high-quality triggers and the correct target label without access to any clean images or prior threat-model knowledge.

A Trojan ticket is defined as a sparse subnetwork $(m\odot\theta)$ obtained by applying iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) to a trained model $\theta$ that was learned on a potentially poisoned dataset $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$, where $m\in\{0,1\}^d$ is the binary pruning mask and $\odot$ denotes elementwise product. The proposed LTH-oriented regime for Trojan analysis uses IMP cycles (train dense model on $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$; prune $p\%$ by magnitude per round; update mask $m$) and examines both (a) the un-rewound pruned subnetwork $(m\odot\theta)$ and (b) its $k$-step finetuned variant $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$ (where $\theta^{(k)}$ denotes $k$ gradient steps of finetuning under $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$, e.g., $k=10$). This regime intentionally avoids using any clean dataset for pruning or finetuning so that the sparsity-induced behavior reflects the interaction between pruning and Trojan-encoded parameters rather than effects of clean-data finetuning.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 1 defines the Trojan ticket concept and the pruning regime. As a methodological definition, it does not contain load-bearing uncertain bridges or highlights. The regime's design choices are operational and their justification is provided by the empirical evidence in conclusions 2–4.

nodes.title: Trojan ticket concept and LTH-based pruning regime for Trojan models

nodes.content: In the specific iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) regime adopted for Trojan analysis — where after each pruning round the surviving weights are not rewound to their initialization and all finetuning uses only the potentially poisoned dataset $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$ (no clean data) — the Trojan score is defined to quantify the pruning-induced stability of Trojan tickets by measuring the linear-mode connectivity (LMC) error barrier between the un-finetuned Trojan ticket $(m\odot\theta)$ and the $k$-step finetuned Trojan ticket $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$. Here, $\theta$ are the parameters of the dense model trained on $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$, $m\in\{0,1\}^d$ is the binary pruning mask, $\odot$ denotes elementwise product, and $\theta^{(k)}$ denotes $\theta$ after $k$ gradient steps of finetuning on $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$. Given a model training error functional $\mathcal{E}(\cdot)$ evaluated on $\mathcal{D}_\mathrm{p}$, the LMC error barrier is $$e_{\sup}(\phi_1,\phi_2)=\max_{\alpha\in[0,1]}\mathcal{E}(\alpha\phi_1+(1-\alpha)\phi_2).$$ Setting $\phi_1 = m\odot\theta$ and $\phi_2 = m\odot\theta^{(k)}$, the Trojan score is $$\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}} \;=\; e_{\sup}(m\odot\theta,\;m\odot\theta^{(k)}) \;-\; \frac{\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta)+\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta^{(k)})}{2}.$$ Under the described IMP regime, the Trojan score is approximately zero for non-Trojan (clean) models because the linear interpolation error barrier equals the average of the endpoints' errors. A significantly positive peak in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ along the pruning path indicates an atypical pruning stability fingerprint associated with a backdoor. Therefore, computing $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ along the IMP pruning path yields a data-free detector that identifies pruning levels where Trojan information is isolated.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 2's detection claim rests on two main premises: P1 (LMC barrier is zero for non-Trojan models under the modified pruning regime) and P2 (k=10 finetuning steps reliably produce a peak). P1 is the more critical risk because it threatens the specificity of the detector; the indirect behavioral evidence from unpoisoned datasets (H3) partially mitigates this, but direct LMC measurement on non-Trojan models under the same regime is missing. P2 is weakened by documented failure cases (2/10 unpoisoned, 3/10 clean-label), indicating that the detection is not universally reliable, especially for clean-label attacks. H1 and H2 support the method's robustness across settings and the choice of k, but they do not eliminate the failure cases. The conclusion is therefore credible in the majority of tested scenarios (especially for basic backdoor attacks) but should not be assumed to hold for all attack variants or random seeds.

nodes.title: LMC-based Trojan score to quantify pruning-induced stability and detect Trojan presence

nodes.content: Empirically, across multiple architectures (ResNet-20s, ResNet-18, VGG-16, DenseNet-100) and datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Restricted ImageNet) and for diverse Trojan types (gray-scale patch, RGB patch, clean-label, stealthier WaNet), there exists an extreme-sparsity subnetwork—termed the winning Trojan ticket—identified by a peak in the Trojan score (the LMC-based metric $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ that quantifies pruning-induced stability via the error barrier between un-finetuned and finetuned Trojan tickets), which simultaneously (i) preserves the Trojan attack effectiveness in terms of attack success rate (ASR) nearly as well as the original dense Trojan model and (ii) has near-random standard accuracy (SA) on clean inputs due to the aggressive pruning. For example, for ResNet-20s on CIFAR-10 with an RGB trigger, at very extreme sparsity the winning Trojan ticket exhibited ASR = 94.49% while SA dropped to 11.38%; across experiments, winning-ticket ASR values reached 99.6% for RGB triggers and 99.8% for clean-label triggers. The winning Trojan ticket is consistently associated with the peak Trojan score along IMP.

metadata.narrative: The existence of a winning Trojan ticket is strongly supported across basic backdoor attacks (H4, H5, H6), with high reproducibility. However, P3 documents non-negligible failure rates for clean-label attacks (30%) and unpoisoned seeds (20%), limiting the claim's universality. H7's transparency about these failures increases credibility by not overstating, but the conclusion must be interpreted as holding in a majority but not all cases under the tested conditions. The highlight H5 (pruning method specificity) strengthens the interpretation that the phenomenon is linked to importance-based sparsity.

nodes.title: Existence of a winning Trojan ticket that preserves attack success under extreme sparsity

nodes.content:
Using the winning Trojan ticket as the victim model in a trigger-recovery optimization
      $$
      \min_{z\in\{0,1\}^n,\;\delta}\; \mathbb{E}_x\big[\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}(x'(z,\delta);\phi,t)\big] + \gamma\,h(z,\delta),
      $$
      with $x'(z,\delta)=(1-z)\odot x + z\odot\delta$, C\&W targeted loss $\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}$, and the regularizer $h$ from prior work, and solving the label-wise optimizations followed by selecting the label with minimum $\|z^*\odot\delta^*\|_1$ recovers (i) the correct Trojan target label more reliably than applying the same optimization to the dense model and (ii) a recovered trigger that, when stamped onto test images, achieves substantially higher ASR. Representative quantitative results: on ResNet-20s, CIFAR-10, (a) gray-scale trigger: recovered ASR = 91.2% (winning ticket) vs 71.4% (dense baseline); (b) RGB trigger: 99.6% vs 48.0%; (c) clean-label trigger: 99.8% vs 9.6% (an over 90%-point ASR improvement reported). The recovered triggers from winning Trojan tickets are effective even when the recovery optimization uses only 100 Gaussian noise images as base inputs (i.e., "for free") rather than any clean images.

metadata.narrative: Conclusion 4's trigger recovery claims are strongly supported by H8 (data-free high ASR), H9 (extensive cross-setting validation), H10 (success in large-class problem), and H11 (visual quality). These highlights consistently show that the winning ticket enables recovery of effective triggers. P4 raises uncertainty about the evaluation victim model; if ASR is evaluated on the winning ticket rather than the original model, the comparison to the dense baseline would be invalid. P5 questions the baseline choice, but the margins (especially for clean-label, 9.6% vs 99.8%) are so large that even a stronger baseline would likely still be substantially worse. The residual risk from P4 requires clarification from the authors, but given standard practice and the visual evidence, the conclusion is credible.

nodes.title: Data-free reverse engineering of triggers using the winning Trojan ticket yields substantially improved target-label detection and recovered-trigger attack success

nodes.content: In the specific IMP-based pruning regime adopted for Trojan models — where after each pruning round the surviving weights are not rewound to their initialization and all finetuning uses only the poisoned dataset (no clean data) — the linear mode connectivity (LMC) error barrier between the resulting un-finetuned Trojan ticket $(m\odot\theta)$ and the $k$-step finetuned Trojan ticket $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$ on the poisoned training set is approximately zero when the model was trained on a clean (unpoisoned) dataset, so that the Trojan score $\mathcal{S}_{\text{Trojan}}= e_{\sup}(m\odot\theta, m\odot\theta^{(k)}) - (\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta) + \mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta^{(k)}))/2$ vanishes for non-Trojan models.Jonathan Frankle, Gintare Karolina Dziugaite, Daniel Roy, and Michael Carbin. Linear mode connectivity and the lottery ticket hypothesis. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pages 3259-3269. PMLR, 2020.

metadata.failure_mode: If the LMC barrier is not approximately zero for non-Trojan models under the modified IMP regime (i.e., $e_{\sup}(m\odot\theta, m\odot\theta^{(k)}) \gg (\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta) + \mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta^{(k)}))/2$), then the Trojan score $\mathcal{S}_{\text{Trojan}}$ would be positive even for clean models. Consequently, the detector would falsely flag a non-Trojan model as containing a backdoor, invalidating the detection claim that the Trojan score is a fingerprint specific to Trojan-infected models. The conclusion that the Trojan score provides a reliable data-free detector would be unsupported for the claimed scope of application because the necessary condition of zero baseline for non-Trojan models would be violated.

refs.text: Jonathan Frankle, Gintare Karolina Dziugaite, Daniel Roy, and Michael Carbin. Linear mode connectivity and the lottery ticket hypothesis. In International Conference on Machine Learning, pages 3259-3269. PMLR, 2020.

metadata.weakness_reason: The paper relies on the result from [19] that IMP subnetworks are linearly connected when the pruning follows the standard LTH pipeline (with weight rewinding and training/retraining on clean data). However, the adopted regime deviates in two key ways: (i) weights are not rewound to the initial values after each pruning round, and (ii) all finetuning is performed on the poisoned dataset rather than on clean data. These differences could break the conditions that allow near-zero LMC barriers. The paper does not directly measure the LMC barrier for non-Trojan models under its own regime; instead, it infers the specificity of the Trojan score from indirect behavioral evidence (the recovery experiments on unpoisoned datasets, which show no false alarms in the recovery pipeline). This leaves open the possibility that non-Trojan models trained and pruned under the same modified regime yield a non-zero Trojan score, causing false positives in backdoor detection.

nodes.title: LMC error barrier is approximately zero for non-Trojan models under the specific IMP regime

nodes.content: Across all experimental conditions involving Trojan models (including ResNet-20s, VGG-16, ResNet-18, DenseNet-100 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, R-ImageNet with gray-scale, RGB, clean-label, WaNet triggers), the choice of $k=10$ gradient steps of finetuning on the poisoned dataset is sufficient to produce a peak in the Trojan score $\mathcal{S}_{\text{Trojan}}$ (the LMC-based measure of pruning stability defined as $\mathcal{S}_{\text{Trojan}} = e_{\sup}(m\odot\theta, m\odot\theta^{(k)}) - (\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta) + \mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta^{(k)}))/2$) at the winning ticket for every replicate, with no failures except in 2 of 10 unpoisoned-seed trials and 3 of 10 clean-label replicates.

metadata.failure_mode: If $k=10$ is not sufficient to produce a peak in some cases (e.g., clean-label attacks), the Trojan score fails to identify the winning ticket, leading to a false negative in detection. The conclusion that the Trojan score can detect Trojan presence would then be unreliable for those attack types. The claim of a "reliable detector" would be weakened to a heuristic with known failure modes.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's ablation (Fig. A7) shows that the success rate of detecting the winning ticket plateaus near 100% for $k \geq 7$, based on ten replicates. However, the failure-case analysis later reveals that in some settings (clean-label and unpoisoned seeds), the detection fails despite using $k=10$, indicating that $k$ alone does not guarantee success. The paper does not investigate whether different values of $k$ would rescue those failures, nor does it provide a procedure for tuning $k$ per model/attack combination in deployment where ground truth is unknown. The reported success rate of 70-80% in those settings contradicts the claim that $k=10$ is sufficient.

nodes.title: k=10 finetuning steps are sufficient to produce a Trojan score peak for Trojan models, with few exceptions

nodes.content: Under the proposed IMP-based pruning regime with $p=20\%$ per round and $k=10$ finetuning steps, the winning Trojan ticket — the extreme-sparsity subnetwork with peak Trojan score (the LMC-based metric $\mathcal{S}_{\text{Trojan}}$) that preserves high ASR (e.g., >94%) while reducing SA to near-random (e.g., <12%) — is consistently found in every trial for every combination of architecture, dataset, and basic backdoor attack, and also in a majority (7/10) of trials for clean-label attacks and in 8/10 of unpoisoned-seed trials.

metadata.failure_mode: If the winning ticket does not exist in a significant fraction of trials (30% for clean-label), then the conclusion that "there exists a winning Trojan ticket" across the claimed configurations is false as a universal statement. It would hold only for a class of attacks and seeds, reducing the practical reliability. The claim that the winning ticket is "consistently associated with the peak Trojan score along IMP" would need to be qualified by a success probability, not asserted as a deterministic relationship.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper's own failure case analysis reports that on clean-label attacks, 3 of 10 replicates with different random seeds fail to locate the winning ticket; on unpoisoned datasets, 2 of 10 seeds trigger a false detection. These fractions (30% and 20%) are non-negligible and contradict a deterministic claim of existence. The paper attributes these failures to randomness but does not explain why the method fails in these cases or provide conditions under which success is guaranteed. Thus, the existence of the winning ticket is not universal but probabilistic, and the conditions for its existence are not fully characterized.

nodes.title: Winning ticket existence not universal across trials

nodes.content: The attack success rates (ASR) of the recovered triggers are computed by using the original dense Trojan model (the one that was given as input to the detection pipeline) as the classifier on test images stamped with the recovered trigger, rather than using the winning ticket itself as the classifier.

metadata.failure_mode: If the ASR values in the tables are computed on the winning ticket rather than the original dense model, then the comparison to the dense baseline is invalid because the baseline's ASR is evaluated on the dense model (as per standard practice). The reported improvements (e.g., 99.6% vs 48.0% for RGB, 99.8% vs 9.6% for clean-label) would be based on different test models. The recovered trigger might be highly effective on the winning ticket but ineffective on the original model, which is the model a defender cares about. The conclusion that the winning ticket enables "substantially improved" trigger recovery would be unsupported in the practical scenario.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper does not explicitly state which model is used to evaluate the ASR of the recovered triggers. In the descriptions of the tables, it simply says "Performance of recovered triggers" and "ASR". In the trigger recovery literature, it is standard to evaluate the recovered trigger on the original Trojan model (since the goal is to demonstrate that the trigger works on the model under inspection). However, the text in Section 5.2.2 says "The recovered trigger pattern ... indeed yields a valid Trojan attack of high ASR" without specifying the victim model. This ambiguity leaves open the possibility that the evaluation was performed on the winning ticket itself, which is known to have high ASR for the true trigger and might be more sensitive to any trigger-like pattern, potentially inflating the reported ASR figures.

nodes.title: Attack success rates of recovered triggers are evaluated using the original dense Trojan model

nodes.content:
The dense baseline method used for comparison, Tabor [32], when applied to the original Trojan model with 100 noise images, achieves ASR of 71.4% for gray-scale trigger, 48.0% for RGB trigger, and only 9.6% for clean-label trigger on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20s. A well-tuned implementation of Neural Cleanse [79] on the dense model under the same base-image conditions would not achieve ASR significantly higher than those Tabor values, especially for the clean-label case.Wenbo Guo et al., Tabor: A Highly Accurate Approach to Inspecting and Restoring Trojan Backdoors in AI Systems, arXiv 2019.
      Bolun Wang et al., Neural Cleanse: Identifying and Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Neural Networks, IEEE S&P 2019.

metadata.failure_mode: If a better-tuned dense baseline (e.g., NC with optimized hyperparameters on noise images) achieves ASR close to the winning-ticket-based recovery (e.g., 95% instead of 48% for RGB, 80% instead of 9.6% for clean-label), then the conclusion of "substantially improved" trigger recovery would be exaggerated. The large margins reported (especially the 90+% point improvement for clean-label) would be artifacts of a weak baseline, and the winning ticket's advantage would be reduced to an incremental improvement in some settings. The practical significance of the method would be diminished.

refs.text: Wenbo Guo et al., Tabor: A Highly Accurate Approach to Inspecting and Restoring Trojan Backdoors in AI Systems, arXiv 2019.
Bolun Wang et al., Neural Cleanse: Identifying and Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Neural Networks, IEEE S&P 2019.

metadata.weakness_reason: The paper chooses Tabor [32] as its dense baseline, but Tabor is not the state-of-the-art trigger recovery method on all attacks. For the clean-label attack, the baseline's ASR is extremely low (9.6%), suggesting that Tabor fails to recover any useful trigger from the dense model for this attack. Neural Cleanse [79], which the paper uses as the optimization backbone, might achieve higher ASR on the dense model if properly tuned (e.g., the paper shows NC with clean images achieves 72.6% ASR for RGB trigger, versus 48% for Tabor with noise images, indicating baseline sensitivity). The paper does not compare against a strong implementation of NC on the dense model under the same noise-image inputs, leaving open the possibility that the improvement is partly due to a weak baseline rather than the winning ticket.

nodes.title: Baseline Tabor method achieves low ASR for clean-label attacks on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20s

nodes.content: The Trojan score $\mathcal{S}_{\text{Trojan}}$ produces a distinct peak in the extreme sparsity regime for Trojan models when evaluated on four architectures (ResNet-20s, ResNet-18, VGG-16, DenseNet-100), three datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, R-ImageNet), and five trigger types (gray-scale patch, RGB patch, clean-label, WaNet, and varying trigger locations), as shown in Figs. 3, 4, A9, A12, and the WaNet appendix.

metadata.credit: This cross-validation preempts the failure mode that the Trojan score peak is an artifact of a specific architecture, dataset, or attack type. Without this wide validation, the detection claim could be dismissed as a narrow empirical coincidence. The multi-dimensional sweep underwrites the generalization claim of conclusion 2: the Trojan score is a fingerprint of Trojan presence across diverse realistic scenarios, not a one-off pattern.

nodes.title: Cross-validation of Trojan score across architectures, datasets, and attack types

nodes.content: An ablation (Fig. A7) on ResNet-20s, CIFAR-10 with RGB triggers varies the number of finetuning steps $k$ from 1 to 12 and measures the success rate of detecting the winning ticket using the Trojan score (from ten replicates per $k$). The success rate rises sharply after $k=3$, exceeds 90% at $k=7$, and plateaus near 100% for $k=10$ and beyond.

metadata.credit: This ablation guards against the failure mode that the detection peak is an arbitrary consequence of choosing a particular finetuning length. It provides empirical grounding that $k=10$ is in the plateau region where detection is stable. Without this, the detection claim would be vulnerable to the criticism that different $k$ yields different peaks and the result is not reproducible. The ablation shows that a broad range of $k$ (7-12) works, making the method robust to small variations.

nodes.title: Ablation of finetuning steps validates choice of k=10

nodes.content: On an unpoisoned CIFAR-10 dataset with clean-trained ResNet-20s, the trigger recovery pipeline (which relies on the winning ticket) yields similar $\ell_1$ norms of recovered triggers across all ten labels (dense baseline: 107-265; winning ticket: 240-476), without any single label showing a distinctly lower norm that would trigger detection (see appendix on un-poisoned datasets).

metadata.credit: This behavioral check provides indirect evidence that the Trojan score (which selects the winning ticket) does not produce a distinct peak on clean models. The failure mode of false positives is preempted: if non-Trojan models produced a low-$\ell_1$ norm on some label, the detector would flag them as backdoored. The similar norms across labels indicate that no such peak occurred. While not a direct LMC measurement, this independent behavioral check strengthens the claim that the Trojan score is specific to Trojan models.

nodes.title: Non-Trojan models produce no false alarm in recovery pipeline

nodes.content: The winning Trojan ticket is experimentally found across four architectures (ResNet-20s, ResNet-18, VGG-16, DenseNet-100), three datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, R-ImageNet), and five attack types (gray-scale, RGB, clean-label, WaNet, varying positions), as shown in Figs. 4, A9, A12, and the WaNet appendix. For example, on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20s, the ticket achieves ASR 94.49% (RGB) and 99.8% (clean-label) while SA drops to 11.38% or below.

metadata.credit: This reproducibility preempts the failure mode that the winning ticket is a peculiarity of a single experimental setup. Without it, the existence claim could be dismissed as an artifact. The multi-dimensional validation underwrites the conclusion's generality, showing that the effect is robust across factors that commonly vary in practice.

nodes.title: Reproducible existence across architectures, datasets, and attack types

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-20s and RGB triggers, three importance-based pruning methods — iterative magnitude pruning (LTH), one-shot magnitude pruning (OMP), and SNIP — all produce a winning Trojan ticket with preserved ASR and near-random SA at extreme sparsity. Random pruning, in contrast, fails to preserve ASR at any sparsity level, as shown in Fig. A10.

metadata.credit: This comparison strengthens the conclusion by ruling out the alternative explanation that any form of sparsity would preserve Trojan features. The failure of random pruning shows that structured selection of important weights is necessary, supporting the interpretation that the winning ticket isolates Trojan-encoded features rather than being a side effect of parameter reduction. Without this, the conclusion would be vulnerable to the criticism that sparsity in general causes the effect.

nodes.title: Other importance-based pruning methods also find the winning ticket; random pruning fails

nodes.content: Visualizations of the loss landscape (Fig. A8) for dense Trojan models and their corresponding winning Trojan tickets on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet show that winning tickets have sharp local minima, in contrast to the flatter minima of dense models.

metadata.credit: This qualitative evidence provides a mechanistic layer that the LMC-based Trojan score (which quantifies the barrier between unfinetuned and finetuned tickets) reflects real landscape geometry. The sharp minima explain why a temporary finetuning (moving away from the sharp minimum) increases the LMC barrier. Without this visualization, the detection method would be purely empirical; the visualizations lend plausibility and help explain why the Trojan score peaks at the winning ticket, strengthening the conclusion's credibility beyond raw empirical correlations.

nodes.title: Loss landscape visualizations support mechanistic rationale

nodes.content: The paper reports failure cases where the LMC-based detection does not locate the winning ticket: 2 of 10 replicates with unpoisoned seeds and 3 of 10 replicates with clean-label attacks, including visualizations of both success and failure cases (Fig. A13).

metadata.credit: Documenting failure cases demonstrates discipline in not overclaiming robustness. It preempts the failure mode that the conclusion is overstated by acknowledging conditions where the phenomenon does not occur. This increases the credibility of the overall empirical claim by showing awareness of limitations, allowing readers to assess reliability.

nodes.title: Failure case analysis documents limitations

nodes.content: Using only 100 noise images from a standard Gaussian as base images in the recovery optimization, the winning Trojan ticket yields recovered triggers with ASR 91.2% (gray-scale), 99.6% (RGB), and 99.8% (clean-label) on CIFAR-10 ResNet-20s, as shown in Table 1.

metadata.credit: This result directly preempts the failure mode that the recovery method requires clean data, which may be unavailable. By demonstrating high ASR with pure noise, the practical utility of the method is established. The high absolute ASR (≥91%) also shows that the recovered trigger is qualitatively meaningful, not just a relative improvement.

nodes.title: Data-free trigger recovery achieves high ASR

nodes.content: The superiority of winning-ticket-based recovery over dense baseline is shown across 6 datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, R-ImageNet, MNIST, GTSRB, YouTubeFace), 5 architectures, multiple attack types, and trigger positions, as compiled in Tables 1, 2, 3, A4, A5, A6, A7.

metadata.credit: This extensive validation preempts the failure mode that the improvement is confined to a narrow setting. The consistent pattern — winning ticket recovers higher ASR, smaller ℓ1 norm, and correct target label across diverse conditions — makes it highly unlikely that the improvement is coincidental. The comparison underwrites the conclusion's claim of general applicability.

nodes.title: Extensive cross-setting validation of trigger recovery improvement

nodes.content: On YouTubeFace (1283 classes) with ResNet-20s and RGB triggers, the dense baseline (Tabor) detects the wrong target label (class "9") with ASR 9.8%, while the winning-ticket-based recovery correctly detects label "1" with ASR 98.7% (Table 2).

metadata.credit: This result is particularly strong evidence because large-class problems are notoriously difficult for trigger recovery. The dense baseline fails completely, while the winning ticket succeeds with high ASR, demonstrating that the improvement can mean the difference between failure and success in challenging realistic scenarios. Without this evidence, the conclusion might be limited to small-class datasets; this case extends the credible regime.

nodes.title: Success on large-class challenging dataset (YouTubeFace)

nodes.content: Fig. 6 shows that triggers recovered from winning Trojan tickets are concentrated, sparse, and resemble the ground-truth trigger (a small white patch in the upper right), while triggers from dense models are diffuse and noisy, for ResNet-20s on CIFAR-10 and ResNet-18 on ImageNet with RGB triggers.

metadata.credit: The visual evidence preempts the failure mode that the recovered trigger, despite high ASR, is a diffuse pattern that would be ineffective or not allow manual verification. The clean visual quality supports the conclusion that the trigger is genuinely recovered, not a spurious optima. It also suggests that the winning ticket's backdoor information is cleanly isolated, lending plausibility to the recovery method's superior performance.

nodes.title: Visualizations confirm quality of recovered triggers

steps.reasoning:
Define the objects and symbols used to state the Trojan-ticket concept. Let $\theta\in\mathbb{R}^d$ denote a trained neural network parameter vector of dimension $d$; let $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{p}}$ denote a possibly poisoned (i.e., Trojan-injected) training dataset; let $m\in\{0,1\}^d$ denote a binary mask whose zero entries indicate pruned weights and whose one entries indicate retained weights; and let the elementwise product symbol $\odot$ denote coordinate-wise multiplication. The pruned subnetwork (a "ticket") is written as $(m\odot\theta)$ and is a function parameterized by the vector obtained from zeroing coordinates of $\theta$ where $m$ has zeros.
[18]

Describe the iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) pipeline adopted from the lottery ticket hypothesis (LTH) and adapted to Trojan analysis. IMP operates in repeated cycles where (i) a network is trained to produce learned parameters $\theta$ from some initialization (commonly denoted $\theta_0$), (ii) a fraction $p\%$ of parameters in $\theta$ are removed by thresholding smallest weight magnitudes to update the mask $m$, and (iii) the mask $m$ is recorded for the current sparsity level and the procedure repeats. In the standard LTH protocol the pruned network is commonly rewound to the initialization $\theta_0$ at each round, but the LTH-oriented regime for Trojan analysis modifies this pipeline as described next to preserve Trojan-encoded information.
[18]

State the specific choices that define the LTH-oriented pruning regime for Trojan analysis. Start from a dense model $\theta$ trained on the possibly poisoned dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{p}}$. Apply iterative magnitude pruning (IMP) cycles that prune $p\%$ of remaining parameters per round by magnitude and update the binary mask $m$. For the purposes of Trojan analysis, do not use any clean (unpoisoned) dataset at any stage of pruning or fine-tuning so that the observed sparsity-induced behaviors reflect interactions between pruning and Trojan-encoded parameters rather than effects of finetuning on clean data. The regime therefore intentionally avoids access to clean data during mask selection and finetuning.
[84]

Distinguish the two pruned-network variants examined under this regime and define notation for finetuning. (a) The un-rewound pruned subnetwork is the final pruned model without resetting or substantial finetuning, denoted $(m\odot\theta)$ where $\theta$ are the parameters obtained from training on $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{p}}$ prior to the final pruning step. (b) The $k$-step finetuned variant is denoted $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$, where $\theta^{(k)}$ denotes the result of applying $k$ gradient-descent steps of finetuning under the same poisoned dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{p}}$ while keeping the mask $m$ fixed (an example choice used in this work is $k=10$). The comparison between $(m\odot\theta)$ and $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$ isolates how pruning alone versus pruning+local optimization under the poisoned data affect Trojan-encoded functionality.
Fig. 1
[18]

Specify auxiliary implementation details used in the pruning regime that are pertinent to reproducing the concept. The per-round pruning ratio $p$ used in IMP cycles in experiments is implemented by removing 20% of the remaining parameters at each prune step (i.e., $p=20\%$ per round following common LTH practice), and the finetuning length choice $k=10$ for $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$ is an empirical selection supported by ablation studies. Also note that in multiple places the authors remark they do not reset the remaining parameters to the original random initialization at the final sparsity—this "un-rewound" choice preserves Trojan properties in $(m\odot\theta)$.
[18]
Fig. 3

Summarize the Trojan-ticket concept and the LTH-oriented regime succinctly from the building blocks above: A Trojan ticket is the sparse subnetwork $(m\odot\theta)$ obtained by applying IMP to a model trained on a potentially poisoned dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{p}}$, with $m\in\{0,1\}^d$ the binary pruning mask and $\odot$ the elementwise product. The LTH-oriented regime inspects both $(m\odot\theta)$ and its $k$-step finetuned variant $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$, while explicitly avoiding the use of any clean data for pruning or finetuning so that sparsity-induced behaviors reveal interactions between pruning and Trojan-encoded parameters.
Fig. 3

Start from the upstream result (conclusion 1) as known: the LTH-oriented regime produces the un-rewound pruned subnetwork $(m\odot\theta)$ and its $k$-step finetuned variant $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$, with all pruning and finetuning performed using only the possibly poisoned dataset $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{p}}$ (no clean data). These two networks serve as the pair whose stability under linear interpolation we will quantify.

Introduce the training error functional and define linear-mode connectivity (LMC) error barrier. Let $\mathcal{E}(\cdot)$ denote the training error (a scalar-valued functional mapping a network parameter vector to its training error on the dataset used for evaluation). Given two networks $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$, define the linear interpolation at scalar $\alpha\in[0,1]$ as $\alpha\phi_1 + (1-\alpha)\phi_2$ (this denotes the network whose parameters are the convex combination of the two parameter vectors). The LMC error barrier between $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$ is then
$$
e_{\sup}(\phi_1,\phi_2)=\max_{\alpha\in[0,1]} \mathcal{E}\big(\alpha\phi_1+(1-\alpha)\phi_2\big),
$$
which is the maximum training error encountered along the linear path between the two networks.
[19]

Specialize the LMC error barrier to the pair of interest and define the Trojan score. Set $\phi_1 = m\odot\theta$ and $\phi_2 = m\odot\theta^{(k)}$ where $\theta$ and $\theta^{(k)}$ are defined as in the LTH-oriented regime. Define the Trojan score $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ as
$$
\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}} \;=\; e_{\sup}(m\odot\theta,\;m\odot\theta^{(k)}) \;-\; \frac{\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta)+\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta^{(k)})}{2}.
$$
The second term is an error baseline formed by the arithmetic mean of the endpoint errors; subtracting it centers the score so that zero indicates that the interpolation barrier matches the endpoint errors.
[19]

Explain the expected behavior of the Trojan score in the non-Trojan (benign) case and the Trojan case. If there is no Trojan attack present in the training data, previous LMC observations imply that the two pruned networks are typically linearly connected without a significant barrier, i.e., $\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta)\approx\mathcal{E}(m\odot\theta^{(k)})\approx e_{\sup}(m\odot\theta,m\odot\theta^{(k)})$, which yields $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}\approx 0$. By contrast, in the presence of a Trojan, the authors assert that the interpolation error barrier can be significantly higher than the endpoints, producing a substantially positive $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$; such a positive peak along the pruning path is interpreted as an atypical pruning-stability fingerprint associated with a backdoor.
[19]
Fig. 3

Argue why computing $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ along the IMP pruning path yields a data-free Trojan detector. The IMP pruning path produces a sequence of masks $m$ and corresponding pruned endpoints $(m\odot\theta)$ and $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$ without requiring any clean dataset; evaluating $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ at each sparsity level therefore identifies sparsity points where the LMC-based barrier is anomalously large. A significantly positive peak in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ serves as an indicator that pruning has isolated parameters that encode the backdoor, hence providing a detector that requires no access to clean training samples.
Fig. 4

Support the detection claim with the warm-up empirical evidence provided. The paper presents a warm-up example where the Trojan score computed between the un-finetuned ticket and the $k$-step ($k=10$) finetuned ticket exhibits a pronounced peak in the extreme-sparsity region, and that peak coincides with preservation of high attack success rate (ASR) for the un-finetuned ticket; this empirical concurrence justifies using $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ as a practically useful, data-free Trojan score.
Fig. 3

Start from the upstream result (conclusion 2) as known: the LMC-based Trojan score $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ identifies pruning levels where the linear interpolation error barrier between $(m\odot\theta)$ and $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$ is anomalously high; treat that score-computation procedure and its interpretation as established.

Describe the experimental scope and configurations used to search for extreme-sparsity subnetworks across models, datasets, and trigger types. The architectures considered include ResNet-20s, ResNet-18, VGG-16, and DenseNet-100; the datasets include CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Restricted ImageNet (R-ImageNet) with 9 classes in R-ImageNet experiments; and the Trojan trigger types examined include gray-scale local patches (BadNets), RGB image-patch triggers, clean-label triggers (crafted by adversarial perturbation of target-class images), and stealthier global warping-based triggers (WaNet). The IMP procedure prunes 20% of remaining parameters per round, and the finetuning length choice $k=10$ is used to form $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$ unless otherwise ablated.
[29]
Fig. 4

State the empirical finding: across these architectures, datasets, and Trojan types, there exists an extreme-sparsity subnetwork—termed the "winning Trojan ticket"—that is identified by a peak in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ along the IMP pruning path. The winning Trojan ticket simultaneously (i) preserves high attack success rate (ASR) comparable to the original dense Trojan model despite extreme sparsity, and (ii) exhibits near-random standard accuracy (SA) on clean inputs because of the aggressive pruning level; hence it isolates Trojan behavior in a minimal set of parameters.
Fig. 3
Fig. 4

Provide concrete empirical examples and numerical values reported in the experiments that substantiate the winning-ticket claim. For ResNet-20s on CIFAR-10 with an RGB trigger, in the extreme-sparsity regime the winning Trojan ticket exhibited ASR $=94.49\%$ while SA dropped to $11.38\%$ (this extreme example is shown in the main pruning dynamics plots). Table 1 reports other winning-ticket ASR values, e.g., $99.6\%$ for the RGB trigger and $99.8\%$ for the clean-label trigger for ResNet-20s on CIFAR-10. The authors further report winning-ticket success across other model/dataset combinations summarized in Table 2, demonstrating that the winning-ticket phenomenon is consistent across the experimental suite.
Fig. 4
Fig. A11

Explain supporting observations that tie the winning Trojan ticket to the Trojan score peak and justify why it is identified at extreme sparsity. In the non-extreme sparsity regime ($p\%<90\%$) both the un-finetuned and finetuned tickets preserve SA and ASR similar to the dense model; in contrast, in the extreme sparsity regime ($p\%>99\%$) the un-finetuned ticket preserves ASR while SA collapses to near-random, and this behavior weakens after finetuning, indicating the sparse pattern itself encodes the Trojan functionality. The peak in $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$ consistently coincides with the sparsity level where ASR remains high but SA is near-random, thereby marking the winning Trojan ticket.
Fig. 4

Note experimental ablations and reproducibility details that reinforce the robustness of the finding. The choice of $k\ge 7$ finetuning steps is sufficient to accurately locate winning Trojan tickets in repeat experiments, different pruning ratios $p$ (e.g., $p=10\%$ or $20\%$ per round) can produce winning tickets while overly aggressive per-round pruning (e.g., $p=40\%$) can fail, and other pruning algorithms (OMP, SNIP) also produce winning Trojan tickets while random pruning does not—these ablations confirm that the winning-ticket phenomenon is not a fragile artifact of a single hyperparameter choice.
Fig. A7
Fig. A9

Begin from the upstream result (conclusion 3) as given: a winning Trojan ticket—a highly sparse subnetwork identified by the peak $\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{Trojan}}$—exists and isolates Trojan behavior. Treat the winning Trojan ticket $(m\odot\theta)$ (and optionally $(m\odot\theta^{(k)})$) as the victim model $\phi$ to be used in reverse-engineering experiments.

State the reverse-engineering optimization problem used to recover a Trojan trigger and its target label. Let $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ denote a base input image; let $z\in\{0,1\}^n$ denote a binary spatial mask encoding positions of the trigger; let $\delta\in\mathbb{R}^n$ denote the trigger pattern; and define the poisoned input as $x'(z,\delta)=(1-z)\odot x + z\odot\delta$. Given a victim model $\phi$ and a putative target label $t$, the trigger-recovery optimization is
$$
\min_{z\in\{0,1\}^n,\;\delta}\; \mathbb{E}_x\big[\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}(x'(z,\delta);\phi,t)\big] + \gamma\,h(z,\delta),
$$
where $\ell_{\mathrm{atk}}(\cdot;\phi,t)$ is a targeted attack loss (specified here as the C\&W targeted attack loss), $h(z,\delta)$ is a regularizer controlling trigger sparsity and smoothness, and $\gamma>0$ is a regularization weight. The binary variable $z$ is relaxed to a convex probabilistic hull to enable optimization, and the optimization is solved separately for each candidate label $t$.
[3]
[79]

Explain the label-selection rule used to infer the Trojan targeted label from the outcome of the label-wise optimizations: for each candidate label $t$ solve the relaxed optimization to obtain $(z^*(t),\delta^*(t))$, compute the $\ell_1$ norm $\|z^*(t)\odot\delta^*(t)\|_1$ of the recovered trigger pattern for that label, and select the detected Trojan target label as the label with minimum recovered trigger $\ell_1$ norm:
$$
t_{\mathrm{Trojan}} \;=\; \arg\min_{t}\; \|z^*(t)\odot\delta^*(t)\|_1.
$$
This follows the minimum-perturbation rationale used in prior reverse-engineering work: a true target label can be achieved by a smaller perturbation if the model contains a backdoor shortcut to that label.
[79]

State the incremental claim under test: using the winning Trojan ticket as the victim model $\phi$ in the above optimization yields (i) more reliable detection of the correct Trojan target label via the minimum-$\ell_1$ criterion and (ii) recovered triggers that, when stamped onto test images, achieve substantially higher attack success rate (ASR) than running the same recovery optimization on the original dense Trojan model. This leverages the observational fact that the winning ticket better isolates the backdoor functionality into a sparse parameter subset, making the trigger optimization landscape easier to exploit.
Fig. 5

Provide the representative quantitative experimental evidence reported. For ResNet-20s on CIFAR-10, when using the winning Trojan ticket as victim model the recovered-trigger attack success rates reported in Table 1 are: (a) gray-scale trigger: recovered ASR = $91.2\%$ for the winning ticket vs $71.4\%$ for the dense baseline; (b) RGB trigger: $99.6\%$ vs $48.0\%$; (c) clean-label trigger: $99.8\%$ vs $9.6\%$ (an over 90 percentage-point improvement for the clean-label case). These numbers quantify both (i) improved target-label detection correctness (the minimum-$\ell_1$ criterion correctly selects the true label more reliably for the winning ticket, as shown by the match indicators in the recovery plots) and (ii) substantially higher ASR of the recovered triggers when recovered from the winning ticket compared to the dense baseline.
Fig. 5
Table 1

State the "for free" recovery claim and the supporting evidence on base-input choice. In the reverse-engineering experiments the base images $x$ used in the optimization were by default 100 random Gaussian noise images drawn from $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ (i.e., no clean images). Table 3 shows that with such noise base images the winning Trojan ticket still yields high-quality recovered triggers (e.g., RGB case: $99.6\%$ ASR when using the winning ticket vs $48.0\%$ for the dense baseline), demonstrating that trigger recovery can be achieved "for free" without access to benign images when the winning ticket is used as the victim model.
Table 3
[80]

Note qualitative and additional empirical corroboration: visualizations of the recovered triggers show that triggers recovered from winning Trojan tickets are more clustered and sparser and produce stronger activation patterns leading to higher ASR when stamped onto test images; these visualizations and numerical ASR improvements together substantiate that the winning-ticket-based recovery yields both better target-label detection and higher recovered-trigger attack success in practice.
Fig. 6

open_questions.content: The authors acknowledge several unresolved scientific and practical issues that remain after this work: (1) computational scalability and efficiency: the LTH-IMP pipeline used to locate winning Trojan tickets is computationally expensive (pruning cycles, repeated training, and LMC evaluations), and scaling the approach to substantially larger and deeper models (e.g., very large ImageNet-scale architectures) requires more efficient algorithms or approximations; (2) failure modes and robustness: there exist documented failure cases (e.g., a non-negligible fraction of trials on some clean-label attacks or random seeds where LMC does not accurately locate the winning Trojan ticket; in appendices the authors report e.g., 3 of 10 clean-label replicates and 2 of 10 unpoisoned-seed trials failing), so the method’s reliability under all attacker variants and randomness seeds is not guaranteed; (3) hyperparameter sensitivity and pruning design choices: the detection and recovery success depend on pruning configuration (e.g., per-round prune fraction $p$, chosen $k$ finetuning steps; the authors observed $p=10\%$ or $20\%$ work while $p=40\%$ can fail) and on the pruning algorithm (random pruning fails while LTH/OMP/SNIP can succeed), leaving open which principled pruning schedules and masks are universally appropriate; (4) mechanistic understanding: while empirical evidence and loss-surface visualizations suggest winning Trojan tickets correspond to sparse connectivity patterns and sometimes sharper minima, a theoretical explanation for why Trojan-encoding features are more stable to extreme magnitude pruning than benign features is not provided; and (5) potential dual-use and operational constraints: the method can be computationally burdensome for routine model inspection and, as admitted, might be misused — practical deployment therefore requires safeguards (licensing, operational constraints) and further study of adversarial countermeasures by attackers who may adapt to sparsity-based detection. These open points are left for future work.
